newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pamela Harriman's life a mix of wealth and power.
newsitem.headline: Pamela Harriman's life a mix of wealth and power.

text.p: Pamela Harriman, who died in Paris on Wednesday of a brain haemorrhage, enjoyed a high-flying life as wife or companion to some of the world's wealthiest and most powerful men.
The former daughter -in-law of Winston Churchill and widow of multi-millionaire Averell Harriman, collapsed on Monday evening in Paris, where she was U.S. ambassador. She was 76.
A naturalised American citizen, she came late to U.S. politics but was born into the tight-knit world of conservative British politics.
Harriman, whose full name was Pamela Digby Churchill Hayward Harriman, was born into the English aristocracy in Farnborough, England, on March 20, 1920.

She was just 19 when she married Randolph Churchill, son of wartime British prime minister Winston Churchill, during World War Two. Randolph, a journalist, was a hard-drinking rake but her father-in-law adored her and she fondly called him "papa".
The couple divorced as the war ended but the marriage produced her only child, Winston Spencer Churchill.
Now a member of the British parliament, he raced to her bedside on Tuesday after she fell ill.
Her second marriage was to Broadway producer and cinema magnate Leyland Hayward in 1960. He died in 1971.
She became a U.S. citizen after marrying her third husband, the late multimillionaire and diplomat Averell Harriman in 1971. He was 80 at the time, 29 years her senior.
The marriage was a reunion of sorts as she had had an affair with Harriman during the war when he was supervising U.S. war aid to Britain at President Franklin Roosevelt's request.

Averell Harriman, who died 15 years later, aged 94, had been heir to a railroad fortune and served as governor of New York, presidential confidant and special ambassador in several U.S. administrations while raising funds for the Democratic party.

Her husband's role and her fondness for throwing huge parties for Washington's rich and powerful, led her to become a major Democratic Party figure in her own right, and she grew in prominence following her husband's death.
Through her husbands and later on her own, she was to meet many of the American political leaders of her time, from John Kennedy to Clinton.

Clinton ran as a Washington outsider in his first presidential campaign in 1992. But after winning the election, one of his first stops in the capital was at a dinner party at Harriman's home in Washington's smart Georgetown neighbourhood.
She had raised millions of dollars for his campaign, and as a reward Clinton made her Washington's envoy to Paris, one of the juiciest of U.S. political plums, in 1993.

After coming to France , Harriman became a popular figure in Paris, admired for her fluent French and her gracious style, though ties between Paris and Washington were often bumpy during her time as ambassador.

France and the United States sparred over alleged U.S. espionage on French soil, the "Europeanisation" of NATO, leadership of the United Nations, influence in Middle East peacemaking and power rivalry in Africa.
But Harriman, who remained on good terms with President Jacques Chirac, was made a Commander of France's Order of Arts and Letters in 1996 for her patronage of fine arts.

Among the men with whom she had close relationships were American publishing magnate John Hay Whitney, CBS broadcaster Edward R. Murrow, Italian industrialist Gianni Agnelli and Aly Khan, the son of the Aga Khan.
A series of recent biographies paint her as a social-climber who avidly pursued the wealthy and the politically powerful.
She was embarrassed late in life by a nasty fight with three generations of Averell Harriman's heirs over their inheritance.
The heirs had accused the ambassador in court of frittering away her late husband's fortune while misleading them about the way she had invested funds she was to manage on their behalf.
Her husband's estate, valued at about $65 million in 1986, had dwindled to barely $3 million by December 1995, when she settled the legal dispute with the heirs.

Harriman collapsed on Monday evening at the Ritz Hotel where she had gone for a swim and was rushed to the American Hospital. After four years in the job, she had been widely expected to retire later this year.
